title: Who Sleeps in the Rice
subtitle: The Legend of Toma of Kurosawa
teaser: Every night in the Kurosawa valley, a rice farmer sang his sons a song and waited for them to stop answering. Now something in a white burial robe walks the duelling rings, still singing, still waiting.

sections.heading: I. The Song They Always Ruined
paragraphs: Every night in the Kurosawa valley, Toma sang his sons the same song, and every night they ruined it.
It was a short song. His mother had sung it to him, and her mother to her, further back than anyone in the valley could count.
Moon in the water, wind in the rice, who is that sleeping, sleeping in the rice?

The children were supposed to answer with their names. Then the father sang it again, softer, and again, softer still, until nobody answered. That was how you knew they were asleep. Then you said what the wind says to the rice, and put out the lamp.
Toma’s sons had never once answered properly.
“A frog,” said Mame, who was four. His real name was Kichisaburō, which was much too big for him.
“A badger,” said Haru, who was eight and should have known better.
“Mame’s feet!”
“Lord Itagaki’s horse!”
“Haru,” said Ayame, their mother, without looking up from her sewing, “you’ll get us all hanged.”
Toma made a face of terrible outrage and sang the whole thing again. Ayame said he sang like a heron with a cold. She said it every night, and every night she stopped sewing to listen.
In the end they always answered, mumbled into the quilt. “Haru.” A long breath. “Mame.” He sang it once more, and nobody answered, and then he said it, very softly, the way the wind says it:
“Shhh.”

Toma was nobody special. He grew rice on four narrow terraces at the top of the valley with his father’s reaping sickle, its blade sharpened so many times it was as thin as a willow leaf. He was good at three things: rice, the song, and staying awake until his sons were asleep.

sections.heading: II. The Gate
paragraphs: On harvest morning the boys tied red ribbons into their father’s hair. That was Mame’s idea. The first sheaf of the harvest always got a red ribbon, so the rice god would know it was his. Mame thought the god should know whose father this was, too.
Toma had promised Haru he could cut the first sheaf this year. Haru was standing on the top terrace with the sickle in both hands when the smoke came up the valley.

Lord Itagaki was at war with his neighbour, whose army was marching north and needed to eat. Itagaki had decided it would not eat in Kurosawa. His soldiers came up the valley road with torches, and the dry harvest went up like paper. They drove the whole village, a hundred and forty people, inside the stockade, so nobody could run to the enemy with a sack of rice. Then they shut the gate, dropped the bar, wound an iron chain through it, and fired the thatch.

Toma found Ayame in the smoke with Mame on her hip and Haru by the wrist. They went to the threshing floor in the middle of the village, where the fire would come last. Everyone else was at the walls. It didn’t matter. The walls were burning.
Ayame looked at him over the boys’ heads. She had never cried where the children could see, and she didn’t now.
“Sing,” she said.
So he sat down on the threshing floor with his sons in his lap and sang. Ayame made a small cracked sound that was nearly a laugh. “Heron,” she said, and put her head on his shoulder.
For once, nobody ruined it.
“Haru,” said Haru, coughing.
“Mame.”
He sang it again.
“Haru.”
He sang it again, softer, the way you are supposed to. Nobody answered. Ayame’s head was heavy on his shoulder, and had been for a while.
“Shhh,” said Toma.
Then he laid them down together, picked up his father’s sickle, and went to the gate.

On the other side stood a soldier named Yohei. He was sixteen, and he had been told to make sure the chain held. He had heard the singing. Now he heard the sickle start on the bar, a thin blade on thick oak, steady as a man cutting rice.
Toward midnight a voice came through the planks, hoarse and very calm.
“Boy. I know you’re there. Open the gate. My sons are asleep. I can carry them.”
Yohei held his spear and didn’t move. Afterwards he told himself he had been too afraid of Lord Itagaki. That was true. It never helped.
The chopping went on until dawn. Then it stopped.

sections.heading: III. Nine Harvest Moons
paragraphs: Nobody came to bury Kurosawa. The enemy army turned back, starving, and Lord Itagaki gave each of his soldiers a silver coin for the victory. Yohei threw his in a river.
When the harvest moon rose over the ash, something stood up where the gate had been.

It was tall and gaunt and very pale, and it wore a long white robe, the kind the living put on the dead. Nobody had dressed it. Nobody had been left to. Its hair hung loose and black to its knees, and two red ribbons were still tied in it. The chain that had held the gate shut hung at its hip, and at the end of the chain swung a reaping sickle as thin as a willow leaf. Green fire crawled along the notches where the blade had bitten into oak all night.
It walked north.

It walked only under the harvest moon, one night a year. In the next valley, farmers woke to find a path cut through their paddies: one straight swath, every stalk laid down in neat rows, the way a careful man cuts. But the ears were empty. Every grain was a grey husk, light as ash, as if something had passed through and taken the life out of it.
The next autumn the swath appeared one valley further north. The autumn after that, one more. It was walking a straight line, and at the end of the line was the castle of Lord Itagaki.

Itagaki laughed the first year. The fourth year, he had priests paper his walls with charms. The sixth, he doubled the guard. The eighth, he stopped sleeping at night and had every gate in the castle barred with oak and chained.
One of the new guards on those gates was a man of twenty-four named Yohei, who had asked for the post. He never told anyone why.

sections.heading: IV. The Ninth Moon
paragraphs: On the ninth harvest moon, the guards on the castle walls heard wind moving through the rice below. But the banners hung straight. There was no wind. Something was coming through the fields, and the stalks were lying down in front of it with the sound stalks make.
Shhh.
The outer gate was barred with an oak beam as thick as a man. The sickle went through it in one stroke. What Toma could not cut in a whole night, it cut in a breath.

The few who watched from the towers and lived never described a fight. It didn’t hurry. The chain went out, the sickle came back, and each time a guard folded quietly at the knees, and the green fire on the blade burned a little brighter. Nobody cried out. There was only the hush.
Yohei was the last man between it and Lord Itagaki’s door. He held his spear in both hands and couldn’t make them stop shaking.
It came down the corridor with its robe dragging and the red ribbons swaying in its hair, and it was humming. He knew the tune. He had heard it every night for nine years, in his sleep.
It stopped in front of him and lifted the sickle. Then it waited. It was waiting, he understood, for an answer.
Yohei dropped the spear. He answered the only way he had ever heard it answered.
“Haru,” he whispered. And then: “Mame.”
The sickle didn’t fall.

For a long moment the green went out of its eyes, and behind it Yohei saw a man’s face: a tired farmer with ash in the creases of his skin, looking at him the way you look at someone you think you know from across a market. Its lips moved. It might have been one of the boys’ names. It might have been its own.
Then the green came back.
It reached out its free hand, cold as river water, and laid it on top of Yohei’s head, the way you settle a child who has woken in the night.
“Shhh,” it said, and went past him through the door.
Yohei sat in the corridor with his back against the wall. He heard Lord Itagaki shout once. After that, nothing but a soft hush, like wind through stalks.
In the morning they found the lord sitting up in his bedding with his eyes open, grey all over and light as straw, like an ear of rice with nothing in it.

sections.heading: V. Hollow Harvest
paragraphs: Everyone thought it would rest after Itagaki. It didn’t. Whatever it had been walking toward, it hadn’t arrived.

Now it walks the duelling rings, and it no longer waits for the harvest moon. Its burial robe drags through the sand and its chain whispers behind it. Every cut takes a little life back, and the green fire burns brighter for it, and the fighter across from it goes a little greyer. When it plants the sickle in the ground, fire bursts up around it in a ring, like a stockade going up, and it stands in the middle, where the fire comes last.
It has forgotten its name. The ribbons haven’t. They are still in its hair, unburned after all that fire, so that whoever is watching will know whose father it is.

Some say it is still harvesting: that Kurosawa lost a hundred and forty lives and a year of rice, and it means to take back every grain, one cut at a time. Others say it goes where the crowds are because crowds have children in them, and it is listening.

Yohei is an old man now. The spring after Itagaki died, he went to the Kurosawa valley and planted rice in the ash: one terrace, then four, then the whole valley. People came. There is a village there again, and its gate has no bar. Yohei has never let anyone put one on.

Every harvest, the first sheaf is tied with a red ribbon and left at the open gate. On the night of the harvest moon, Yohei sits beside it and sings the old song into the dark, and answers it himself, two names, one after the other. Some years, the villagers say, the rice by the gate lies down without any wind.

But in the rings, nobody answers. After every cut it asks, so quietly that only the one in front of it can hear: who is that sleeping, sleeping in the rice? And it waits, the way a father waits in the dark for two small voices to ruin his song.
Nobody ruins it anymore. So it does what you do when the answers stop. It tells them what the wind tells the rice.
“Shhh…”
